unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the fundamental difference between Computer Architecture and Computer Organization?

options.text: Architecture refers to programmer-visible attributes (instruction set, data types, addressing modes); Organization refers to operational units and interconnections realizing the architecture (signals, interfaces, memory tech)
Architecture deals with software; Organization deals with hardware casing
Organization is designed by programmers; Architecture by hardware builders
There is no difference between the two terms

explanation: Computer Architecture defines the logical abstraction seen by the machine-language programmer (ISA). Computer Organization describes the low-level microarchitectural implementation that realizes those architectural specifications.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the defining concept of the Von Neumann Computer Architecture?

options.text: Stored-Program Concept: programs (instructions) and data are stored together in the same unified read-write memory address space
Separate physical memories for code and data
Elimination of the Program Counter register
Execution of instructions in reverse order

explanation: The Von Neumann architecture features a single shared memory containing both program instructions and data, executed sequentially via a Program Counter.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: How does the Harvard Architecture differ from the Von Neumann Architecture?

options.text: Harvard uses physically separate storage and signal pathways (buses) for instructions and data
Harvard has no CPU registers
Harvard does not support arithmetic calculations
Harvard is an analog computer system

explanation: Harvard architecture physically separates instruction memory from data memory, allowing simultaneous instruction fetch and operand read/write.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What are the four primary functional components of a classic digital computer?

options.text: Central Processing Unit (CPU), Main Memory Unit, Input/Output Subsystem, and System Bus
Monitor, Keyboard, Mouse, and Printer
Compiler, Assembler, Linker, and Loader
Hard Drive, Flash Drive, CD-ROM, and Magnetic Tape

explanation: The digital computer consists of: CPU (Datapath + Control Unit), Memory Unit, I/O devices, and System Interconnect Bus.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What are the three distinct functional buses that compose the System Bus?

options.text: Data Bus, Address Bus, and Control Bus
Serial Bus, Parallel Bus, and USB
Internal Bus, External Bus, and Local Bus
Read Bus, Write Bus, and Execute Bus

explanation: The system bus comprises: Data Bus (bidirectional, carries data words), Address Bus (unidirectional from CPU, specifies memory addresses), and Control Bus (transmits timing and command signals).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: If an address bus has 16 lines (16-bit address bus), what is the maximum directly addressable memory capacity (assuming byte-addressable memory)?

options.text: 64 KB (2^16 bytes = 65,536 bytes)
1 MB
16 KB
4 GB

explanation: With k address lines, the CPU can directly address 2^k distinct memory locations: 2^16 = 65,536 bytes = 64 KB.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the function of the Program Counter (PC) register in the CPU?

options.text: Holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched and executed
Counts the total number of errors in the program
Stores the result of the last ALU operation
Holds the instruction currently being decoded

explanation: The Program Counter points to the next instruction in sequence; it is automatically incremented after each instruction fetch unless a branch occurs.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the function of the Memory Address Register (MAR)?

options.text: Holds the physical address in memory currently being read from or written to
Stores the data word read from RAM
Stores the processor status word flags
Contains the opcode being decoded

explanation: MAR is connected directly to the address bus lines; it holds the address operand during memory read and write operations.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the function of the Memory Data Register (MDR) / Memory Buffer Register (MBR)?

options.text: Holds the data word read from memory or waiting to be written to memory
Holds the address of the next subroutine
Counts clock cycles
Stores keyboard input bytes

explanation: MDR/MBR connects directly to the bidirectional data bus, acting as a holding buffer between high-speed CPU registers and slower main memory.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the function of the Instruction Register (IR)?

options.text: Holds the machine instruction word fetched from memory while it is being decoded by the control unit
Holds the loop counter
Stores interrupt vectors
Performs integer addition

explanation: Once fetched from memory into MDR, the instruction is loaded into the IR, where its opcode and operand fields are decoded.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the Accumulator (AC) register?

options.text: A general-purpose register associated with the ALU that implicitly stores one of the operands and receives the result of arithmetic/logic operations
A register that accumulates dust inside the CPU
A register that counts clock seconds
A register that stores the BIOS code

explanation: In accumulator-based processor architectures, AC holds intermediate computational results and serves as default operand source/destination.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the purpose of Temporary Register (TR) in basic computer organization (Mano Machine)?

options.text: Holds temporary data during microoperations to avoid overwriting user registers
Stores the system time
Buffers network packets
Stores the bootloader password

explanation: TR is an internal CPU register used by the control unit to hold intermediate scratchpad values during multi-step instruction execution cycles.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What are the sequential phases of the classic Instruction Execution Cycle?

options.text: Fetch instruction -> Decode opcode -> Read effective address (if indirect) -> Execute instruction -> Check for interrupts
Write to disk -> Compile code -> Power off
Decode -> Execute -> Fetch -> Store
Input -> Print -> Restart -> Halt

explanation: The instruction cycle continuously loops through: Fetch (PC to MAR, read memory to IR, increment PC), Decode, Effective Address calculation, Execution, and Interrupt handling.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is a 'Microoperation' in computer organization?

options.text: An elementary operation performed on data stored in one or more registers during a single clock cycle
A tiny computer chip
An instruction written in Python
A mechanical switch movement

explanation: Microoperations are the lowest-level atomic hardware operations (e.g., register transfer, shift, increment, clear) that compose an ISA machine instruction.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is Register Transfer Language (RTL)?

options.text: A symbolic notation used to describe the microoperations and internal data transfers among computer registers (e.g., R2 <- R1 + R3)
A high-level programming language like C
A language spoken by computer repair technicians
A database query syntax

explanation: RTL provides a standardized mathematical notation to specify register transfers, ALU operations, and control conditions concisely.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What does the RTL statement: 'T2: MAR <- PC, PC <- PC + 1' mean?

options.text: At clock timing state T2, transfer contents of PC to MAR, and simultaneously increment PC by 1
Add MAR and PC together
Clear both MAR and PC to zero
Jump to subroutine at address T2

explanation: The statement describes concurrent microoperations occurring at clock pulse T2: transferring the fetch address to MAR and incrementing PC.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is a 'Common Bus System' in CPU internal architecture?

options.text: A shared set of parallel conductive lines that interconnects multiple registers, ALU, and memory, using multiplexers or tri-state buffers to prevent bus contention
A USB cable shared by computers
A city transit network
A serial RS-232 cable

explanation: A common bus multiplexes internal transfers: at any single clock pulse, only one register places its contents onto the bus, while one or more destination registers load from it.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is a 'Tri-State Buffer' and why is it used in bus design?

options.text: A digital logic gate with three output states: Logic 0, Logic 1, and High-Impedance (Hi-Z / disconnected)
A buffer that stores three bytes of data
A buffer with three power supplies
A circuit that multiplies voltages by 3

explanation: Tri-state buffers allow multiple register outputs to connect physically to the same bus line; disabling the buffer disconnects the output (Hi-Z), preventing short circuits.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What are the two fundamental design methodologies for the CPU Control Unit?

options.text: Hardwired Control Unit and Microprogrammed Control Unit
Analog Control Unit and Digital Control Unit
Static Control Unit and Dynamic Control Unit
Synchronous Control Unit and Asynchronous Control Unit

explanation: Control Units are either Hardwired (fixed combinational logic circuits, decoders, state machines) or Microprogrammed (control software/firmware stored in ROM).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the primary operational advantage of a 'Hardwired Control Unit'?

options.text: Ultra-fast execution speed because control signals are generated directly by physical combinational logic gates
Ease of modifying or adding new instructions after manufacturing
Very low chip silicon area for complex instruction sets
It requires no clock oscillator

explanation: Hardwired control produces control signals with minimal gate propagation delay, delivering maximum clock speeds (standard in RISC processors).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the primary operational advantage of a 'Microprogrammed Control Unit'?

options.text: High flexibility and ease of maintenance: instruction sets can be updated, extended, or emulated simply by updating the microcode in ROM
It runs 10 times faster than hardwired logic
It requires zero transistors
It eliminates the need for main memory

explanation: Microprogramming structures the control unit like a tiny CPU inside the CPU: changing or fixing instruction semantics requires only changing the microprogram in control ROM.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: In a microprogrammed control unit, where is the microcode firmware stored?

options.text: Control Memory (Control ROM / PROM)
L1 Data Cache
Hard Drive MBR
Virtual Memory Swap space

explanation: Microcode routines reside in a dedicated high-speed internal read-only memory known as Control Memory.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the function of the Control Address Register (CAR)?

options.text: Holds the address of the next microinstruction to be read from Control Memory
Holds user array addresses
Counts CPU clock cycles
Stores disk track sectors

explanation: CAR functions as the 'program counter' of the control unit, pointing to the active microinstruction in control store.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the function of the Control Data Register (CDR) / Control Buffer Register (CBR)?

options.text: Holds the microinstruction read out from control memory while its control word fields are active
Buffers network packets
Stores floating-point numbers
Holds the keyboard buffer

explanation: CDR holds the current microinstruction, whose control fields directly drive the enable lines, ALU function select, and next-address logic.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the difference between 'Horizontal Microcode' and 'Vertical Microcode'?

options.text: Horizontal microcode uses wide, unencoded control words where each bit controls a specific hardware signal directly; Vertical microcode uses compact, encoded fields requiring decoders
Horizontal runs on PCs; Vertical on mainframes
Horizontal is written in binary; Vertical in hex
There is no difference

explanation: Horizontal microcode offers high parallelism (many functional units active simultaneously) at the cost of wide microinstructions. Vertical microcode saves ROM width by encoding actions into fields.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is an 'Opcode' (Operation Code)?

options.text: The binary portion of a machine instruction that specifies the mathematical or logical operation to be performed (e.g., ADD, SUB, LOAD)
The memory address of the operand
The serial number of the CPU
A comment in assembly language

explanation: The opcode specifies *what* operation the processor must execute on the operands.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: If an instruction word is 16 bits wide, with 4 bits allocated for Opcode and 12 bits for Memory Address, how many distinct operations can the CPU support?

options.text: 16 distinct operations (2^4 = 16)
4 operations
4096 operations
64 operations

explanation: With n bits for opcode, the CPU supports 2^n distinct operation codes: 2^4 = 16 operations.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: For the same 16-bit instruction with 12 bits of address, what is the maximum addressable memory in words?

options.text: 16 words
65,536 words
1,024 words

explanation: A 12-bit address field directly addresses 2^12 = 4096 memory words.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the role of the 'Addressing Mode' bit (I) in basic computer instruction formats?

options.text: Specifies whether the operand address in the instruction is Direct (I = 0) or Indirect (I = 1)
Marks the instruction as illegal
Inverts the result of the ALU
Indicates whether the CPU is in user mode

explanation: In basic computer design (Mano), the most significant bit (bit 15) indicates direct addressing (0) or indirect memory addressing (1).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is 'Effective Address' (EA)?

options.text: The actual physical memory address where the operand is located, or where program control is transferred to
The address of the compiler
The address of the CPU on the motherboard
The size of the cache in bytes

explanation: Effective address is the resolved physical memory address computed by applying the instruction's addressing mode rules.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: In Indirect Addressing, how many memory accesses are required during the instruction cycle to fetch a single operand?

options.text: 2 memory accesses (first to read the effective address pointer from memory, and second to read the actual operand)
1 memory access
3 memory accesses
Zero memory accesses

explanation: First access reads the address pointer stored in memory; the second access fetches the actual data operand from that effective address.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is a 'General Purpose Register' (GPR) Organization?

options.text: A CPU datapath architecture where multiple general-purpose registers (R0, R1, ..., Rn) can serve as sources and destinations for any ALU operation
A computer with no RAM
A system where all registers are read-only
An architecture with only an Accumulator

explanation: GPR architectures (standard in modern x86, ARM, RISC-V) replace single accumulator bottlenecks with flexible multi-register register files.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: In a GPR bus organization with 7 general-purpose registers, an ALU, and an external bus, what selects the source registers A and B and destination register C?

options.text: A Control Word comprising multiplexer selection fields (SELA, SELB, SELD, and ALU Operation OPR)
A hardware key
The power supply voltage
The screen resolution

explanation: The Control Word fields drive multiplexer select inputs to route chosen source registers to the ALU inputs and latch the result into the destination register.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is an 'Arithmetic Microoperation'?

options.text: Microoperations that perform basic arithmetic calculations on numeric values (e.g., Add, Subtract, Increment, Decrement)
Operations that compare text strings
Operations that invert bits
Operations that reboot the PC

explanation: Arithmetic microoperations execute numeric operations: R3 <- R1 + R2, R1 <- R1 + 1, R1 <- R1 - 1, etc.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the 2's complement representation of subtraction R1 - R2 in terms of basic microoperations?

options.text: R1 + R2' + 1 (where R2' is 1's complement of R2)

explanation: In digital logic, binary subtraction is performed by adding the 2's complement of the subtrahend: R1 - R2 = R1 + (~R2) + 1.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is a 'Logic Microoperation'?

options.text: Bitwise operations performed on strings of bits stored in registers (e.g., AND, OR, XOR, NOT)
Evaluating algebraic polynomials
Solving differential equations
Calculating square roots

explanation: Logic microoperations manipulate individual bit positions independently, treating registers as arrays of binary flags.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: Which logic microoperation is used to SELECTIVELY CLEAR (reset to 0) specific bits in register A using a mask in register B?

options.text: A <- A AND B' (or A AND NOT B)
A <- A OR B
A <- A XOR B
A <- A + B

explanation: ANDing register A with the complement of mask B clears those bits in A where B has 1s, leaving other bits unchanged (Selective Clear).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: Which logic microoperation is used to SELECTIVELY SET (set to 1) specific bits in register A using a mask in register B?

options.text: A <- A OR B
A <- A AND B
A <- A XOR B
A <- NOT A

explanation: ORing register A with mask B sets to 1 all bit positions where B has 1s, preserving all other bits (Selective Set).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: Which logic microoperation is used to SELECTIVELY INVERT (toggle / complement) specific bits in register A?

options.text: A <- A XOR B
A <- A AND B
A <- A OR B
A <- NOT B

explanation: XORing with 1 flips the bit (0^1=1, 1^1=0); XORing with 0 preserves the bit (Selective Complement).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What are the three types of Shift Microoperations?

options.text: Logical Shift, Arithmetic Shift, and Circular (Rotate) Shift
Fast Shift, Slow Shift, Medium Shift
Integer Shift, Float Shift, Double Shift
Read Shift, Write Shift, Clear Shift

explanation: Shift microoperations are: Logical (shifts in 0), Arithmetic (preserves sign bit), and Circular / Rotate (recirculates shifted-out bits back into opposite end).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: In a Logical Shift Right (SHR), what binary value is always inserted into the most significant bit (MSB) position?

options.text: The previous sign bit
The bit shifted out of the LSB

explanation: Logical shift always injects zero into the vacant extreme bit position (0 into MSB for SHR; 0 into LSB for SHL).

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: In an Arithmetic Shift Right (ASHR), what binary value is copied into the most significant bit (MSB)?

options.text: The sign bit is retained (MSB remains unchanged and is duplicated)
Always 0
Always 1
The LSB value

explanation: Arithmetic shift right divides a signed 2's complement number by 2: to preserve the algebraic sign, the sign bit (MSB) is copied into itself and the adjacent position.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: In an Arithmetic Shift Left (ASHL), what potential condition must be detected?

options.text: Arithmetic Overflow (if the sign bit changes after shifting left)
Divide by zero
Underflow
Parity loss

explanation: Multiplying a signed number by 2 via ASHL causes overflow if the bit shifted out of bit n-1 differs from the new sign bit, altering the sign.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What does Circular Shift (Rotate) Right (ROR) do with the bit shifted out of the least significant bit (LSB)?

options.text: Inserts it into the most significant bit (MSB) position
Discards it permanently
Stores it in the Accumulator
Sets the zero flag to 1

explanation: Rotate operations wrap bits circularly: the bit leaving the LSB re-enters at the MSB.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is a 'Bus Arbitration' protocol?

options.text: A mechanism that decides which bus master device (CPU, DMA controller) gets control of the shared system bus when multiple devices request it simultaneously
A protocol that speeds up memory chips
An encryption system for bus data
A tool for counting data bytes

explanation: Bus arbitration arbitrates competing master requests using daisy-chaining, centralized priority arbiters, or distributed arbitration.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is 'Daisy Chaining' in bus arbitration?

options.text: A serial hardware connection where a bus grant signal propagates sequentially from the highest priority device to lower priority devices
Connecting multiple hard drives in parallel
Wiring memory chips in a circular ring
A software loop in the BIOS

explanation: In daisy-chaining, the device closest to the central arbiter intercepts the grant line if it requested the bus; otherwise it passes the grant downstream to lower-priority devices.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is the function of the Status / Flags Register in the CPU?

options.text: Holds individual 1-bit condition flags (Zero flag Z, Sign flag S, Carry flag C, Overflow flag V) set by ALU operations
Stores the computer brand name
Holds the monitor resolution
Tracks total hours powered on

explanation: The Flags register records status conditions resulting from the most recent ALU instruction, used by conditional jump/branch instructions.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: When is the Zero Flag (Z) set to 1?

options.text: When the result of the last arithmetic or logical operation equals exactly zero
When the CPU clock is halted
When memory is empty
When an interrupt occurs

explanation: If all bits of the ALU output are 0, the Zero Flag Z is asserted (Z = 1); otherwise Z = 0.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: What is an 'Instruction Decoder' circuit in the control unit?

options.text: A combinational logic decoder (e.g., 3-to-8 or 4-to-16 decoder) that activates a unique output control line corresponding to the binary opcode
A program that translates French to English
A software compiler
A memory RAM tester

explanation: The instruction decoder converts the binary n-bit opcode into one of 2^n active control pathways to initiate the required sequence of microoperations.

unit_title: Basic Organization, CPU Registers & Control Unit
prompt: Why is the Control Unit often described as the 'Brain' of the Central Processing Unit?

options.text: It fetches, decodes, and orchestrates the timing and sequence of all data transfers, register updates, and ALU operations across the computer
It performs all multiplication and division
It contains the permanent storage media
It provides the power supply

explanation: While the ALU executes operations, the Control Unit directs and coordinates every subsystem, generating the precise control pulses that drive the machine.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What are the four common instruction format architectures classified by the number of memory addresses they specify?

options.text: Three-Address, Two-Address, One-Address (Accumulator), and Zero-Address (Stack) Instructions
16-bit, 32-bit, 64-bit, and 128-bit instructions
Serial, Parallel, Synchronous, and Asynchronous instructions
Integer, Float, Double, and String instructions

explanation: ISAs are classified by explicit address operand fields: 3-address (X = A + B), 2-address (X = X + B), 1-address (AC = AC + M), and 0-address (TOS = TOS + SOS via Stack).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In a 'Three-Address Instruction' format, what do the three address fields represent in an operation like: ADD R1, A, B?

options.text: Destination register (R1), First source operand (A), and Second source operand (B)
Three different memory addresses added together
Three opcodes executed in parallel
Three clock cycles

explanation: Format: [Opcode, Dest, Source1, Source2]. R1 <- M[A] + M[B]. It provides expressive concise code at the expense of wide instruction words.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In a 'Two-Address Instruction' format, what occurs in the operation: ADD R1, R2?

options.text: R1 <- R1 + R2 (Destination register R1 also serves as one of the source operands)
R1 and R2 are both cleared
Result is placed in R0

explanation: In two-address format [Opcode, Dest/Src1, Src2], the destination register is implicitly overwritten with the result.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In a 'One-Address Instruction' format (Accumulator machine), how is the instruction ADD X executed?

options.text: AC <- AC + M[X] (The Accumulator register is an implicit operand and destination)
Memory location X is added to itself
AC is cleared to zero

explanation: One-address instructions specify only one explicit memory operand; the second operand and destination are implicitly the Accumulator register.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: How does a 'Zero-Address Instruction' format (Stack machine) perform an ADD operation?

options.text: Pops the top two elements from the Stack, adds them in the ALU, and pushes the result back onto the Top of Stack
Adds zero to the program counter
Adds zero to all registers
Executes an instruction with no clock cycles

explanation: In a stack architecture (Zero-Address), instructions like ADD, SUB require no explicit operand addresses because operands are implicitly at Top of Stack (TOS).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What are 'Reverse Polish Notation' (RPN) or Postfix Expressions, and why are they used in Zero-Address stack computers?

options.text: Operators follow their operands (e.g., A B +), eliminating the need for parentheses and operator precedence rules during stack evaluation
Expressions written in Polish characters
Expressions read backwards from right to left
Mathematical expressions that use no numbers

explanation: Postfix RPN allows simple left-to-right linear stack evaluation: push operands until an operator arrives, then pop operands, evaluate, and push result.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: Convert the infix expression (A + B) * (C - D) into Postfix (RPN) form:

options.text: A B + C D - *
A B C D + - *
* + A B - C D
+ A B * - C D

explanation: (A + B) becomes 'A B +'; (C - D) becomes 'C D -'. Multiplying the two terms places the '*' operator at the end: 'A B + C D - *'.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What are the three general categories of computer instructions based on function?

options.text: Data Transfer Instructions, Data Manipulation Instructions, and Program Control Instructions
Fast, Medium, and Slow Instructions
User, System, and Kernel Instructions
Source, Binary, and Executable Instructions

explanation: Instructions divide into: 1. Data Transfer (MOV, LOAD, STORE, PUSH, POP), 2. Data Manipulation (Arithmetic, Logic, Shift), and 3. Program Control (JMP, CALL, RET, Branches).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: Which of the following is a 'Program Control Instruction'?

options.text: JUMP / BRANCH / CALL / RETURN
ADD / SUB
AND / OR
LOAD / STORE

explanation: Program control instructions alter the sequential flow of program execution by loading new target addresses into the Program Counter (PC).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is the primary purpose of 'Addressing Modes' in computer architecture?

options.text: To provide flexibility for pointer manipulation, array indexing, and dynamic program relocatability while reducing the number of address bits in instruction words
To determine the speed of the CPU clock
To format hard drive partitions
To connect to internet IP addresses

explanation: Addressing modes allow programmers to reference large memory spaces, traverse arrays, access pointer data structures, and write position-independent code efficiently.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Immediate Addressing Mode', where is the operand located?

options.text: Directly inside the instruction word itself (as an operand field constant)
In main memory at address 0
In a general purpose register
On the hard disk drive

explanation: In immediate addressing, the operand value is part of the instruction (e.g., MOV R1, #25), requiring zero memory access cycles to fetch data.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Direct Addressing Mode' (Absolute Addressing), what does the instruction address field contain?

options.text: The exact effective physical memory address of the operand (EA = Address field)
The operand value itself
The address of a pointer
The register number only

explanation: Direct addressing provides the actual memory address directly: Effective Address EA = A (e.g., LOAD AC, 5000 loads contents of memory address 5000).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Indirect Addressing Mode', what does the instruction address field contain?

options.text: The memory address where the effective address of the operand is stored (EA = M[A])
The operand data
A relative branch offset
The register opcode

explanation: Indirect addressing implements pointers: the address field points to a memory location that contains the actual address of the operand.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Register Addressing Mode', where is the operand located?

options.text: Inside a designated CPU register (EA = R)
In main memory RAM
In the instruction cache
On the stack

explanation: In register mode, the operand resides in a CPU register specified by a small k-bit register select field, executing at register speeds.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Register Indirect Addressing Mode', what does the designated register contain?

options.text: The memory address of the operand (EA = [R])
The operand data value
An instruction opcode
A interrupt vector

explanation: The register holds a memory pointer: EA = (R). Data is fetched from memory at the address stored in register R (e.g., MOV A, @R0).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Relative Addressing Mode' (PC-Relative), how is the Effective Address computed?

options.text: EA = PC + Address Offset (Displacement)
EA = Base Register + Index Register
EA = M[PC]
EA = Address field - PC

explanation: PC-relative addressing adds a signed offset to the current Program Counter: EA = PC + offset. It is widely used for short relative branch and jump instructions.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is the primary advantage of Relative (PC-Relative) Addressing?

options.text: Enables Position-Independent Code (PIC): the entire program code can be loaded anywhere in physical memory without recalculating branch targets
It requires zero bits in the instruction
It allows infinite RAM size
It eliminates the ALU

explanation: Because jumps are relative offsets (+12, -8) from the current PC rather than hardcoded absolute addresses, the program executes identically regardless of where in memory it is loaded.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Indexed Addressing Mode', how is the Effective Address computed?

options.text: EA = Base Address + Contents of Index Register (XR)
EA = XR - Base
EA = M[Base] * XR
EA = XR / 2

explanation: Indexed mode computes EA = A + XR. Incrementing the index register XR sequentially traverses elements of an array starting at base address A.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Base Register Addressing Mode', how is the Effective Address computed?

options.text: EA = Contents of Base Register (BR) + Displacement / Offset
EA = BR * Offset
EA = BR - PC
EA = M[BR]

explanation: Base-register addressing adds an instruction displacement to a designated Base Register, enabling dynamic segment relocation by the operating system.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What occurs in 'Auto-Increment Addressing Mode'?

options.text: The effective address is the register contents; after accessing the operand, the register is automatically incremented by the data size
The register is incremented before accessing memory
The program counter is doubled
All registers are incremented simultaneously

explanation: In auto-increment (e.g., (R1)+), operand address is R1; subsequently, R1 is automatically incremented to point to the next array item or stack element.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What occurs in 'Auto-Decrement Addressing Mode'?

options.text: The register is decremented by the data size FIRST, and the new decremented value is then used as the effective address
The register is decremented after reading data
The register is multiplied by -1
Data in memory is decremented

explanation: In auto-decrement (e.g., -(R1)), R1 is decremented prior to memory access, mirroring stack push operations.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: Which pair of addressing modes naturally implements Push and Pop operations on a downward-growing Stack?

options.text: Auto-Decrement for PUSH and Auto-Increment for POP
Immediate for PUSH and Direct for POP
Relative for PUSH and Indexed for POP
Indirect for both

explanation: PUSH predecrements stack pointer SP and stores data (-SP). POP reads data and postincrements SP (SP+).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What does 'RISC' stand for in computer architecture?

options.text: Reduced Instruction Set Computer
Random Instruction Storage Controller
Reliable Integrated System Core
Redundant Interface System Computer

explanation: RISC is a microprocessor design philosophy favoring a small set of simple, uniform, highly optimized instructions.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What does 'CISC' stand for in computer architecture?

options.text: Complex Instruction Set Computer
Central Integrated System Controller
Compact Instruction Sequential Core
Cascaded Instruction Storage Circuit

explanation: CISC provides a rich, varied set of complex instructions (variable length, multi-cycle, memory-to-memory operations).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: Which of the following is a fundamental design characteristic of RISC architectures?

options.text: Load/Store Architecture: only dedicated LOAD and STORE instructions access main memory; all ALU operations occur strictly between registers
Complex variable-length instructions with multiple memory operands
Microprogrammed control units with massive control ROMs
Small register sets (fewer than 8 registers)

explanation: RISC mandates that ALU instructions operate exclusively on registers (Load/Store architecture), decoupling memory access from arithmetic processing.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: Which of the following is a hallmark characteristic of CISC architectures (e.g., Intel x86)?

options.text: Variable-length instruction formats, many addressing modes, and instructions capable of performing memory-to-memory operations directly
All instructions execute in a single uniform clock cycle
Purely hardwired control unit
Absence of stack operations

explanation: CISC architectures support rich instruction sets with variable byte lengths (1 to 15 bytes in x86) and complex memory operands.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: Why do RISC processors typically feature large Register Files (e.g., 32 to 128 general-purpose registers)?

options.text: To keep frequently used variables in fast CPU registers, minimizing slow main memory access latency
Because RISC chips have no RAM
To store the microcode ROM
To store the operating system kernel on chip

explanation: Because RISC relies on register-to-register operations, large register files reduce memory bus traffic and instruction cycle delays.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In Berkeley RISC, what hardware mechanism is used to pass function parameters between subroutines with zero memory overhead?

options.text: Overlapping Register Windows
Hardware Stack Pointer
DMA transfer
Shared L3 cache

explanation: Register Windows partition the register file into overlapping sets (Input, Local, Output), allowing the caller's output registers to become the callee's input registers seamlessly.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is 'Instruction Pipelining' in modern CPU architecture?

options.text: A hardware technique where multiple instructions are overlapped in execution, like an assembly line, across distinct hardware stages
Storing instructions in oil-filled pipes
Sending instructions over fiber optic cables
Executing one instruction after another strictly sequentially

explanation: Pipelining divides instruction execution into discrete stages (Fetch, Decode, Execute, Writeback), overlapping successive instructions to increase instruction throughput.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is 'Superscalar Architecture'?

options.text: A processor capable of fetching, decoding, and executing MULTIPLE independent instructions simultaneously per clock cycle using multiple parallel execution pipelines
A processor that runs faster than light
A CPU with more than 1000 cores
A computer with multiple monitors

explanation: Superscalar CPUs contain redundant execution units (multiple ALUs, FPUs), executing Instructions-Per-Cycle (IPC) > 1.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is 'Simultaneous Multithreading' (SMT), known commercially as Intel Hyper-Threading?

options.text: A hardware technique that allows a single physical processor core to appear as two or more logical cores by duplicating register state while sharing execution units
Running two programs on two different computers
Splitting an executable file into two halves
Running code without an operating system

explanation: SMT duplicates architectural register sets and program counters per thread on a single physical core, hiding memory stalls by interleaving instructions from multiple threads into idle pipeline slots.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is a 'Multi-Core Microprocessor'?

options.text: A single integrated circuit die containing two or more independent, complete physical CPU execution cores
A computer with multiple motherboards
A CPU that has multiple power cables
A processor that only runs multi-threaded code

explanation: Multi-core processors integrate multiple discrete processing cores onto a single silicon chip, sharing lower-level cache (L3) and memory controllers.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is the function of the L3 (Level 3) Cache in modern multi-core processors?

options.text: A large, on-chip cache shared equally by all CPU cores to facilitate fast inter-core communication and cache sharing
A cache stored on the hard drive
A backup cache stored in the BIOS ROM
A cache for web pages

explanation: Modern CPUs dedicate private L1 and L2 caches to individual cores, while providing a massive shared on-die L3 cache across all cores.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is 'Intel QuickPath Interconnect' (QPI) or AMD Infinity Fabric?

options.text: High-speed, point-to-point coherent packet-based bus links connecting processors, memory controllers, and I/O hubs, replacing the legacy Front Side Bus (FSB)
A software utility for overclocking
A wireless Wi-Fi antenna inside the CPU
A SATA hard drive connector

explanation: Modern multi-socket servers use point-to-point interconnects (QPI, UPI, Infinity Fabric) for high-bandwidth, low-latency inter-socket cache-coherent communication.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is 'Endianness' in computer data representation?

options.text: The byte ordering convention used to store multi-byte data words in computer memory
The size of the hard drive at the end of the partition
Whether the CPU is installed on the left or right side of the board
A type of network termination

explanation: Endianness defines whether the most significant byte (Big-Endian) or least significant byte (Little-Endian) is stored at the lowest memory address.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Little-Endian' byte ordering (standard in x86/ARM processors), how is the 32-bit hex value 0x12345678 stored starting at memory address 1000?

options.text: Address 1000: 0x78; 1001: 0x56; 1002: 0x34; 1003: 0x12 (Least significant byte at lowest address)
In random byte order

explanation: Little-Endian stores the Little End (least significant byte 0x78) at the lowest memory address.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: In 'Big-Endian' byte ordering (used in internet network protocols), how is 0x12345678 stored starting at address 1000?

options.text: Address 1000: 0x12; 1001: 0x34; 1002: 0x56; 1003: 0x78 (Most significant byte at lowest address)
Address 1000: 0x00

explanation: Big-Endian stores the Big End (most significant byte 0x12) at the lowest memory address (network byte order).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What does 'Subroutine Call' (CALL) instruction do in terms of CPU register operations?

options.text: Pushes the return address (contents of Program Counter PC) onto the Stack, and loads the target subroutine address into PC
Clears all general registers
Halts the processor
Copies the stack to disk

explanation: CALL saves the return address to the stack (or link register) so execution can resume seamlessly upon encountering a RETURN instruction.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What does the 'RETURN' (RET) instruction do?

options.text: Pops the return address from the top of the stack and restores it into the Program Counter (PC)
Resets the CPU to factory settings
Returns zero to the compiler
Deletes the subroutine from memory

explanation: RET pops the saved return address from TOS into PC, redirecting CPU execution back to the caller instruction immediately following CALL.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is a 'Recursive Subroutine' in assembly and stack architecture?

options.text: A subroutine that calls itself directly or indirectly, requiring dynamic stack frames for each activation to maintain local variables and return pointers
A subroutine with an infinite loop
A subroutine that never uses the stack
A subroutine that deletes its own code

explanation: Recursion relies on the hardware stack to allocate private activation frames (call frames) for each invocation depth.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is the 'Condition Code' (CC) generation in the ALU?

options.text: Hardware comparator logic that evaluates arithmetic results and updates flags: Negative (N), Zero (Z), Overflow (V), Carry (C)
Generating passwords for BIOS
Testing hardware voltage levels
Writing compiler diagnostic codes

explanation: ALU operations inherently produce condition flags indicating whether the result was zero, negative, produced an unsigned carry, or signed 2's complement overflow.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: Under what condition does Signed Overflow (V = 1) occur during the addition of two numbers?

options.text: When two positive numbers are added and produce a negative result, or two negative numbers are added and produce a positive result
Whenever there is a carry out of the MSB
When the result equals zero
When one number is positive and the other is negative

explanation: Overflow occurs if and only if the carry into the sign bit differs from the carry out of the sign bit: V = C_in XOR C_out.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is an 'Unconditional Branch' instruction?

options.text: A jump instruction that ALWAYS alters the Program Counter (PC <- Target Address) regardless of any condition flags
A jump that only occurs on zero
A branch that occurs randomly
A branch that halts the CPU

explanation: Unconditional jumps (e.g., JMP 2000) execute without evaluating status flags, transferring control unconditionally.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is a 'Conditional Branch' instruction?

options.text: A jump instruction that inspects specific status flags (e.g., JZ - Jump if Zero, JC - Jump if Carry) and branches only if the test is satisfied
A branch that requires user permission
A jump that occurs only on Tuesdays
A jump executed by hardware reset

explanation: Conditional jumps evaluate status flags (e.g., if Z == 1, then PC <- target; else PC advances normally).

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is 'Memory-Mapped I/O'?

options.text: I/O device registers are mapped into the same address space as main memory RAM, accessed using standard memory instructions (LOAD, STORE)
I/O devices connected with HDMI cables
Displaying hard drive sectors on the monitor
Mapping RAM addresses to web URLs

explanation: In memory-mapped I/O, peripheral registers appear as regular memory addresses; no specialized I/O instructions are needed.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is 'Isolated (Port-Mapped) I/O'?

options.text: I/O devices have a separate address space from memory, requiring specialized CPU instructions like IN and OUT to communicate with device ports
I/O devices isolated in physical Faraday cages
Devices connected only via Bluetooth
I/O without power supply

explanation: Isolated I/O (e.g., Intel x86 IN/OUT instructions) uses dedicated hardware control lines (IOR/IOW vs MEMR/MEMW) to separate I/O port addresses from memory addresses.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is an 'Interrupt' in CPU operation?

options.text: A hardware signal or software event that temporarily suspends the currently executing program and transfers control to an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR)
A broken wire on the motherboard
A computer monitor turning off
A typing error on the keyboard

explanation: Interrupts enable asynchronous events (keystrokes, disk transfers, timer alarms) to receive prompt CPU attention without wasteful polling.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What is an 'Interrupt Service Routine' (ISR)?

options.text: A specialized kernel software routine executed in response to a specific hardware or software interrupt request
A hardware maintenance manual
A background thread that cleans RAM
A compiler diagnostic tool

explanation: The ISR services the interrupting device, reads/writes device buffers, resets interrupt flags, and restores saved CPU state before returning.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: What CPU register saves the state of condition flags and execution mode during an interrupt?

options.text: Processor Status Word (PSW) / Flags Register
Accumulator
Memory Address Register
Program Counter only

explanation: The PSW stores condition flags, CPU privilege mode bit, and interrupt mask bits; it is pushed to the stack upon interrupt entry and restored via IRET.

unit_title: CPU Functioning, Instruction Formats & Addressing Modes
prompt: Why is the instruction fetch-decode-execute cycle called the 'Von Neumann Bottleneck'?

options.text: Throughput is fundamentally constrained by the speed and bandwidth of the shared bus connecting the high-speed CPU to slower main memory
The CPU fan causes air turbulence
Cables are too long
Hard drives are louder than CPUs

explanation: Because CPU clock speeds evolved far faster than memory bus bandwidth, transferring instructions and data across the single Von Neumann bus creates a major performance bottleneck.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the fundamental economic and physical trade-offs represented in the Memory Hierarchy pyramid?

options.text: As we move up the hierarchy (closer to CPU): Speed increases, Cost per bit increases, and Storage capacity decreases
As we move up: Speed decreases and capacity increases
Cost per bit is constant across all tiers
All memory levels have identical access latency

explanation: The memory pyramid trades off capacity against access latency: internal CPU registers and caches are ultra-fast but expensive and small; secondary storage is massive and cheap but orders of magnitude slower.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the standard tiers of the computer Memory Hierarchy ordered from fastest to slowest?

options.text: CPU Registers -> L1 Cache -> L2 Cache -> L3 Cache -> Main Memory (RAM) -> Solid State Drive (SSD) -> Magnetic Hard Disk (HDD) -> Magnetic Tape
Magnetic Tape -> RAM -> Cache -> Registers
Main Memory -> Cache -> Registers -> Disk
HDD -> SSD -> RAM -> Registers

explanation: Hierarchy levels transition from sub-nanosecond register files and on-die SRAM caches to nanosecond DRAM, microsecond flash, and millisecond mechanical disks.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the primary physical difference between Static RAM (SRAM) and Dynamic RAM (DRAM)?

options.text: SRAM uses flip-flops (typically 6 transistors per cell) and needs no refreshing; DRAM uses a single transistor and capacitor per cell and requires periodic refreshing
SRAM loses data when power is turned off; DRAM never loses data
DRAM is 100 times faster than SRAM
SRAM is used for hard drives; DRAM for caches

explanation: SRAM cells store charge in bistable latches (faster, lower density, higher cost, used for caches). DRAM stores charge in capacitors that leak over time, requiring refresh cycles every few milliseconds (used for main RAM).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the primary difference between ROM and RAM?

options.text: ROM is non-volatile (retains data when power is off); RAM is volatile (loses data when power is lost)
ROM can be rewritten millions of times per second; RAM cannot
RAM is read-only; ROM is random-access
There is no difference in volatility

explanation: ROM (Read-Only Memory) stores permanent startup firmware (BIOS/UEFI); RAM (Random Access Memory) provides volatile workspace for active programs.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What distinguishes EEPROM and Flash Memory from older EPROM chips?

options.text: EEPROM and Flash can be erased and reprogrammed electrically in-circuit without requiring ultraviolet (UV) light exposure
EEPROM requires UV light for 30 minutes
EPROM can only be written once at the factory
Flash memory is volatile

explanation: EPROM requires removal and intense UV light to erase floating gate charges. EEPROM and NAND/NOR Flash use Fowler-Nordheim electrical tunneling for fast in-place rewrites.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Coincident Decoding' (2D Memory Decoding) in memory chip architecture?

options.text: Using two decoders (Row decoder and Column decoder) to select a memory cell at the intersection (X, Y), reducing the total number of decoder gate pins
Decoding two instructions at the same time
Using two address buses in parallel
Reading from two hard drives simultaneously

explanation: Coincident decoding arranges memory cells in a 2D matrix: an n-bit address is split into row and column addresses, requiring 2 * 2^(n/2) gate inputs instead of 2^n, dramatically simplifying chip pinout.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Associative Memory' (Content Addressable Memory - CAM)?

options.text: Memory accessed simultaneously by data content rather than by explicit physical numerical address
Memory that associates user accounts with passwords
Memory connected to hard drives via USB
A relational database in RAM

explanation: CAM hardware compares an input search word against all stored words in parallel within a single clock cycle, returning the matching address or status flag (ideal for TLB and routing tables).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What fundamental computational principle enables small cache memories to provide high hit ratios (>95%)?

options.text: Principle of Locality of Reference (Temporal Locality and Spatial Locality)
Amdahl's Law
Moore's Law
Nyquist Theorem

explanation: Programs access a relatively small localized portion of address space at any given time (temporal: recently referenced data reused soon; spatial: nearby addresses accessed sequentially).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is a 'Cache Hit' vs a 'Cache Miss'?

options.text: A Cache Hit occurs when requested data is found in the cache; a Cache Miss occurs when data is absent and must be fetched from lower-level memory
A Cache Hit occurs when RAM is full
A Cache Miss is a hardware error in the memory bus
Cache Hit means the CPU is overheating

explanation: If data is in cache (Hit), it is delivered in 1-4 clock cycles. If missing (Miss), execution stalls while the line is fetched from main memory (Miss Penalty, 50-200 cycles).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the 'Hit Ratio' (h) of a cache memory system?

options.text: The ratio of total cache hits to total memory access requests: h = Hits / (Hits + Misses)
The ratio of cache size to RAM size
The number of clock cycles per hit
The percentage of dirty blocks in cache

explanation: Hit ratio h (expressed as decimal or percentage) measures cache efficiency. Miss ratio m = 1 - h.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the three standard cache mapping techniques?

options.text: Direct Mapping, Fully Associative Mapping, and Set-Associative Mapping
Linear Mapping, Binary Mapping, and Tree Mapping
Serial Mapping, Parallel Mapping, and Bus Mapping
Static Mapping, Dynamic Mapping, and Swapped Mapping

explanation: The 3 mapping techniques dictate where a main memory block can reside in cache: Direct (exactly 1 line), Fully Associative (any line), or Set-Associative (any line within a specific set).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: In 'Direct Mapping', how is the cache line index determined for a memory block with address j?

options.text: Line Index = j mod (Total Number of Cache Lines)
Line Index = j * Total Cache Lines
Line Index = j + Total Cache Lines
Line Index is selected randomly

explanation: Direct mapping maps block j to line (j mod N). Each memory block can go to only one specific cache line, making hardware fast and simple but vulnerable to conflict misses.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the three address fields in Direct Mapped Cache addressing?

options.text: Tag, Line (Index), and Word (Block Offset)
Base, Limit, and Offset
Segment, Page, and Frame
Row, Column, and Channel

explanation: A physical address splits into: Tag (identifies specific memory block), Line/Index (selects which cache line to check), and Word/Offset (selects the byte within the block).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is a 'Conflict Miss' (Collision Miss) in direct-mapped caches?

options.text: Two or more frequently accessed memory blocks map to the exact same cache line, repeatedly evicting each other even though other cache lines are empty
Two CPU cores trying to write to the same register
A memory bus short circuit
A page fault on disk

explanation: Conflict misses occur when multiple active blocks contend for the same line index, causing thrashing (e.g., alternating between block 0 and block N).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: In 'Fully Associative Mapping', where can a memory block be placed in the cache?

options.text: In ANY available cache line anywhere in the cache
Only in line 0
Only in lines that match its address mod 4
Only in the L3 cache

explanation: Fully associative cache allows any memory block to reside in any line, eliminating conflict misses entirely at the cost of requiring parallel tag comparators for every line.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the two address fields in Fully Associative Cache addressing?

options.text: Tag and Word (Block Offset)
Index, Tag, and Offset
Base and Limit
Page and Frame

explanation: Because a block can be anywhere, there is no line index field; the address consists only of a wide Tag and Word offset.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'K-Way Set-Associative Mapping'?

options.text: Cache is divided into Sets, each containing K cache lines; a memory block maps to a specific set (block mod Sets) and can reside in ANY of the K lines in that set
A cache with K processors
A cache that runs K times faster
A cache that stores K-bit numbers

explanation: Set-associative combines direct mapping speed with associative flexibility: block maps to set (j mod S) and can occupy any line in that set (e.g., 2-way, 4-way, 8-way).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the 'Write-Through' cache update policy?

options.text: Every write to the cache is simultaneously written to main memory, keeping main memory constantly consistent with cache
Writes are delayed until the computer reboots
Writes are stored only in CPU registers
Writes are written only to disk

explanation: Write-through ensures memory consistency by updating RAM on every write, but consumes substantial memory bus bandwidth.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the 'Write-Back' (Copy-Back) cache update policy?

options.text: Writes update ONLY the cache line initially; main memory is updated only when the dirty cache line is evicted during block replacement
Writes bypass the cache completely
Writes are sent over the network
Writes are written backwards from end of block

explanation: Write-back minimizes bus traffic by writing to cache at full CPU speed, using a 'Dirty Bit' to track whether the block must be written back to RAM upon eviction.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What does the 'Dirty Bit' in a Write-Back cache line indicate?

options.text: Indicates whether the data in the cache line has been modified by the CPU and differs from the corresponding copy in main memory
Marks corrupted hardware memory cells
Indicates that the line is empty
Marks a line that cannot be read

explanation: If Dirty Bit = 1, the cache block has been modified and must be written back to RAM before replacement; if 0, it can be discarded with zero write overhead.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the Least Recently Used (LRU) cache replacement policy?

options.text: Evicts the cache line within the set that has not been accessed for the longest period of time
Evicts the first block that was loaded into the set
Evicts a block chosen at random
Evicts the smallest block

explanation: LRU tracks access recency, replacing the block that has been idle longest, exploiting temporal locality.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the First-In, First-Out (FIFO) cache replacement policy?

options.text: Evicts the block that has resided in the cache set for the longest time, regardless of how recently it was accessed
Evicts the newest block
Evicts blocks with even addresses
Evicts blocks with errors

explanation: FIFO uses a simple circular queue to evict the oldest resident block, requiring less hardware than LRU but potentially evicting heavily used data.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is a 'Cold Miss' (Compulsory Miss) in cache operation?

options.text: The very first time a memory block is referenced and must be fetched into cache from memory
A miss caused by low CPU temperatures
A miss caused by power loss
A miss due to full cache capacity

explanation: Compulsory (cold) misses are unavoidable initial misses occurring because blocks have never been brought into cache before.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is a 'Capacity Miss' in cache systems?

options.text: A miss that occurs because the cache cannot contain all the blocks needed during execution of a program (working set exceeds total cache size)
A miss due to conflict on the same line index
A miss caused by small address buses
A miss on an empty hard drive

explanation: Capacity misses occur in fully associative caches of finite size when active working set data exceeds total cache capacity.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the '3 Cs' of cache misses?

options.text: Compulsory (Cold), Capacity, and Conflict misses
Compute, Cache, and Control misses
Cost, Current, and Clock misses
Core, Chip, and Circuit misses

explanation: Mark Hill classified cache misses into: Compulsory (first reference), Capacity (cache size limit), and Conflict (mapping collisions in direct/set-associative).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: If cache access time is 2 ns, main memory access time is 50 ns, and hit ratio is 0.95, what is the Average Memory Access Time (AMAT)?

options.text: 4.5 ns
2.5 ns

explanation: AMAT = Hit Time + (Miss Rate * Miss Penalty) = 2 ns + (1 - 0.95) * 50 ns = 2 + 0.05 * 50 = 2 + 2.5 = 4.5 ns.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Cache Invalidation'?

options.text: Marking a cache line as invalid (Valid Bit = 0) so that future references treat it as a miss and fetch fresh data from memory
Formatting the CPU cache
Erasing the BIOS firmware
Deleting files on disk

explanation: Cache lines are invalidated during DMA transfers or multi-core writes to prevent the processor from using stale data.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the 'Cache Coherence Problem' in multi-core symmetric multiprocessors (SMP)?

options.text: Multiple processor cores have private caches holding conflicting, inconsistent copies of the exact same memory variable
Cores running at different clock frequencies
Caches running out of power
Hard drives failing to read sectors

explanation: When Core A writes to variable X in its private L1 cache, Core B's private L1 cache contains an obsolete, stale copy of X unless a cache coherence protocol intervenes.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the two major classes of Cache Coherence Protocols in multiprocessors?

options.text: Snooping Protocols (Bus-Snarfing over shared broadcast bus) and Directory-Based Protocols (Centralized/Distributed state directory)
SRAM and DRAM protocols
RAID 0 and RAID 1 protocols
TCP and UDP protocols

explanation: Snooping broadcasts changes on a shared bus (ideal for small SMPs). Directory protocols maintain sharing lists in memory directories (scalable to hundreds of nodes).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: In the classic MESI cache coherence protocol, what do the four letters stand for?

options.text: Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid
Memory, Execute, Store, Instruction
Microprocessor, Enable, Synchronize, Interrupt
Master, Endpoint, Slave, Interface

explanation: MESI defines 4 line states: Modified (dirty, only in this cache), Exclusive (clean, only in this cache), Shared (clean, in multiple caches), and Invalid (stale/empty).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Direct Memory Access' (DMA) and why is it essential for high-throughput secondary storage?

options.text: Allows peripheral controllers to transfer data blocks directly to/from main memory without constant CPU involvement, interrupting the CPU only upon completion
Accelerates CPU clock speed
Enables wireless data transfer
Protects memory against viruses

explanation: DMA avoids wasting millions of CPU cycles on byte-by-byte polling transfers during high-speed disk or network streaming.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the two common modes of DMA data transfer?

options.text: Burst Mode (Block Transfer) and Cycle Stealing Mode
Fast Mode and Slow Mode
Serial Mode and Parallel Mode
Read-Only Mode and Write-Only Mode

explanation: Burst mode transfers an entire block continuously while holding the bus; Cycle Stealing transfers one word per CPU memory cycle, interleaving with CPU execution.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Cycle Stealing' in DMA operation?

options.text: The DMA controller takes control of the system bus for a single memory cycle to transfer one word, briefly pausing the CPU if it needs the bus
Stealing electricity from the motherboard
Clock cycles stolen by background viruses
Overclocking the memory bus

explanation: In cycle stealing, the DMAC steals occasional bus cycles during instruction fetch or internal ALU phases without freezing the CPU for extended periods.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What internal registers are maintained inside a standard DMA Controller (DMAC)?

options.text: Address Register, Word Count Register, and Control/Status Register
Accumulator, Program Counter, Instruction Register
Base, Limit, Segment registers
Row, Column, Bank registers

explanation: Address register holds memory target; Word Count decrements after each transfer until zero; Control register sets transfer direction (read/write).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What are the physical dimensions or coordinates of a magnetic hard drive platter?

options.text: Cylinders, Tracks, and Sectors (CHS addressing)
Pixels, Vectors, and Lines
Rows, Columns, and Tables
Pages, Frames, and Blocks

explanation: HDD geometry is structured into concentric circular Tracks on Platters, matching vertically aligned tracks across platters as Cylinders, subdivided into angular Sectors.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is a 'Track' on a magnetic disk platter?

options.text: A concentric circular magnetic ring on the surface of a spinning platter where data bits are recorded
The physical edge of the metal casing
The motor spindle
A cable on the motherboard

explanation: Platters are magnetically formatted into thousands of microscopic concentric rings called tracks.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is a 'Cylinder' in magnetic hard drive geometry?

options.text: The set of all circular tracks across all platter surfaces that are located at the exact same radial distance from the spindle center
A round battery on the board
The motor that spins the disk
A protective metal cover

explanation: All read/write heads move together on a shared arm assembly: all tracks under all heads at any given position form a single cylinder.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is a 'Sector' in disk geometry, and what is its typical standard capacity?

options.text: The smallest physical addressable unit of storage on a track, traditionally 512 bytes (or 4096 bytes / 4Kn in Advanced Format)
A partition containing the operating system
A track containing bad blocks
An optical lens

explanation: Sectors are pie-slice subdivisions along tracks, traditionally formatted to store 512 bytes plus ECC error check codes.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Rotational Latency' in disk performance?

options.text: The time required for the desired disk sector on the spinning platter to rotate under the read/write head
The time to spin the motor from standstill to 7200 RPM
The time to eject a CD tray
The time to format the drive

explanation: Average rotational delay is half the time of one complete platter revolution (e.g., 4.17 ms at 7200 RPM).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Seek Time' in disk performance?

options.text: The mechanical time taken by the actuator arm to position the read/write head over the target cylinder
The time to search for a word in a file
The time to download a file from Google Drive
The time to boot the computer

explanation: Seek time is the slowest physical mechanical step in disk I/O, typically ranging between 3 ms and 10 ms.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'NAND Flash Memory' used in Solid State Drives (SSDs)?

options.text: Non-volatile semiconductor storage where floating-gate or charge-trap transistors store bits in organized Pages and Erasure Blocks
Volatile SRAM chips with battery backup
A magnetic disk platter spinning at high speed
An optical laser storage technology

explanation: NAND flash provides fast solid-state electronic storage organized into pages (e.g., 4-16 KB for read/write) and blocks (e.g., 2-8 MB for erase).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: Why can NAND flash NOT perform in-place overwriting of data?

options.text: Flash cells can be programmed (written) at the page level, but can only be erased at the larger Block level (Erase-Before-Write constraint)
Flash memory is read-only
Flash drives are magnetic
Flash cannot store zeros

explanation: NAND flash requires an entire block of hundreds of pages to be erased (reset to 1s) before any page in that block can be rewritten (Programmed to 0s).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the 'Flash Translation Layer' (FTL) in an SSD controller?

options.text: Firmware that maps logical block addresses (LBA) to physical flash pages, handles wear leveling, garbage collection, and bad block management
A driver for SATA cables
A graphics rendering layer
A program to format flash drives

explanation: The FTL emulates a standard block hard drive interface while managing out-of-place writes, block erasures, and wear leveling transparently.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Garbage Collection' in SSD operation?

options.text: Consolidating valid pages from fragmented blocks into a fresh block and erasing the old blocks to reclaim free write capacity
Deleting old user files automatically
Removing temporary internet files
Cleaning dust from cooling fans

explanation: Because overwrites happen out-of-place, garbage collection reclaims blocks full of invalid pages by copying surviving valid pages and issuing block erase.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Write Amplification Factor' (WAF) in SSD performance?

options.text: The ratio of physical bytes written to the flash memory to the logical bytes requested to be written by the host OS (WAF >= 1)
The sound volume produced by writing data
The speedup factor of write caches
The number of files saved per second

explanation: Because garbage collection rewrites valid pages during block compaction, actual flash writes exceed host writes: WAF = (Bytes written to Flash) / (Bytes written by Host).

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is the difference between SLC, MLC, TLC, and QLC flash memory?

options.text: The number of bits stored per individual flash cell: SLC (1 bit), MLC (2 bits), TLC (3 bits), QLC (4 bits)
The physical size of the flash chip
The color of the printed circuit board
The manufacturer brand name

explanation: Higher bit density per cell (TLC/QLC) increases storage capacity and lowers cost, but reduces write endurance (P/E cycles) and write speed.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Optical Memory' (CD, DVD, Blu-ray)?

options.text: Storage media where digital data is read and written using focused laser beams reflecting off microscopic pits and lands on a polycarbonate disc
Memory that uses human eyes to read data
Storage made of glass lenses
A computer monitor screen

explanation: Optical discs use laser reflection changes across microscopic surface indentations (pits and lands) to represent binary 0s and 1s.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'Dual-Channel Memory Architecture' on motherboards?

options.text: Using two independent memory bus channels simultaneously to double the theoretical data transfer bandwidth between RAM and the memory controller
Using two RAM sticks of different sizes
Running RAM in two directions
Using RAM as a hard drive

explanation: Dual-channel doubles the bus width from 64 bits to 128 bits, allowing simultaneous memory read/write across matched pairs of RAM modules.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: What is 'DDR SDRAM' (Double Data Rate Synchronous DRAM)?

options.text: Memory that transfers data on BOTH the rising edge and falling edge of the clock signal, doubling data rate at the same bus clock frequency
Memory that has two power cords
RAM that duplicates every stored file
Memory that runs at 2 Hz

explanation: DDR transfers data twice per clock cycle (on both clock transitions), delivering double the bandwidth of legacy single-data-rate SDR SDRAM.

unit_title: Memory Organization, Hierarchy & Cache Architecture
prompt: Why is Memory Organization considered a critical pillar of Computer Architecture?

options.text: Because system performance, power consumption, and responsiveness are fundamentally limited by the speed and bandwidth of memory access
Because memory is the most expensive part of a computer
Because without memory, the monitor cannot turn on
Because operating systems cannot be written in C without memory

explanation: The 'Memory Wall' dictates modern system efficiency: CPU pipelines stall if memory subsystems cannot supply instructions and operands at the rate execution units consume them.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: Why can Peripheral I/O devices NOT be connected directly to the CPU system bus without an I/O Interface?

options.text: Due to vast disparities in operating speed, data transfer rates, signal formats, word lengths, and operating modes between CPU and peripherals
Because peripheral devices have no electric power
Because the CPU bus is made of copper
Because peripheral cables are too long

explanation: An I/O interface bridges electrical, timing, and protocol discrepancies: CPUs operate at gigahertz electronic speeds, while peripherals are often electromechanical or operate at kilohertz speeds.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What are the primary functional responsibilities of an I/O Interface Unit?

options.text: Data buffering, control and status reporting, address decoding, and electrical signal/format conversion
Compiling high-level programs
Executing machine language instructions
Cooling the CPU socket

explanation: The I/O interface synchronizes data flow between high-speed CPU buses and slower peripherals, converts serial/parallel data, and monitors device status flags.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Programmed I/O' (Polling)?

options.text: The CPU periodically and repeatedly checks the device status register in a busy-wait loop until the device is ready for data transfer
The CPU delegates all work to a dedicated coprocessor
The device interrupts the CPU when ready
Data is transferred wirelessly

explanation: In programmed I/O, the CPU remains trapped in a polling loop waiting for device readiness, wasting massive CPU cycles that could execute user threads.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the primary operational disadvantage of Programmed I/O?

options.text: Severe CPU underutilization: the high-speed CPU wastes valuable processing cycles constantly polling slow peripheral status flags
It requires expensive hardware controllers
It can only handle text data
It causes hard drive crashes

explanation: Polling ties up the processor in busy-waiting loops, making it unacceptable for multitasking operating systems.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: How does 'Interrupt-Initiated I/O' overcome the inefficiency of Programmed I/O?

options.text: The CPU issues an I/O command and continues executing other tasks; the interface hardware raises an interrupt signal ONLY when the device is ready
It speeds up the peripheral motor
It replaces the device with software
It stores all data in ROM
