explanation: Interrupt-driven I/O allows the CPU to perform useful work asynchronously, servicing the peripheral only when interrupted by a hardware ready signal.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a 'Vectored Interrupt'?

options.text: The interrupting device directly supplies an interrupt vector address (or index) to the CPU over the data bus to locate its specific ISR
An interrupt that has magnitude and direction in 3D space
An interrupt generated only by vector supercomputers
An interrupt that cannot be masked

explanation: In vectored interrupts, the peripheral identifies its service routine by placing its vector address on the bus; in non-vectored interrupts, the CPU jumps to a fixed hardwired address.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a 'Non-Vectored Interrupt'?

options.text: The interrupt branch address is fixed and hardwired in the CPU architecture; the ISR must poll devices to determine who requested service
An interrupt that cannot be turned off
An interrupt caused by software bugs
An interrupt with zero priority

explanation: In non-vectored interrupts, all interrupt requests branch to a single predefined memory address where a polling routine identifies the interrupting device.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Daisy-Chaining' in priority interrupt systems?

options.text: A serial hardware connection where an Interrupt Acknowledge (INTA) signal propagates sequentially through devices in descending priority order
Connecting peripherals in a circle
A software linked list of interrupt handlers
Connecting power cables in series

explanation: Daisy-chaining connects devices in series: the device electrically closest to the CPU has the highest priority. If it requested an interrupt, it intercepts INTA and places its vector on the bus; otherwise it passes INTA downstream.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the main drawback of Daisy-Chaining priority resolution?

options.text: Propagation delay: in systems with many devices, the signal takes significant time to traverse the chain, limiting scalability
It requires 64 wires per device
It cannot assign priorities
It only works with printers

explanation: Hardware propagation delay accumulates through each gate in the daisy-chain; if the chain is long, interrupt response time degrades.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Parallel Priority Interrupt' resolution?

options.text: Using a Priority Encoder circuit to evaluate multiple interrupt request lines simultaneously in parallel
Using two CPUs to handle interrupts
Running two ISRs at the exact same instant
Connecting all interrupt wires to ground

explanation: A parallel priority system feeds interrupt request lines into an n-bit priority encoder chip, instantly outputting the binary code of the highest-priority active request.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the function of the 'Interrupt Mask Register' in priority interrupt hardware?

options.text: Allows the CPU to selectively enable (unmask) or disable (mask/block) specific interrupt levels under program control
Hides the interrupt from the user screen
Encrypts interrupt vector addresses
Stores the CPU serial number

explanation: By setting or clearing bits in the mask register, the operating system can prevent low-priority interrupts from interrupting critical kernel sections.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is an 'I/O Channel' or 'Input-Output Processor' (IOP)?

options.text: A specialized autonomous processor with its own instruction set (Channel Programs) dedicated entirely to managing I/O operations independently of the main CPU
A physical wire inside a USB cable
A channel on a television
A software chat room between processes

explanation: Pioneered in IBM mainframes, IOPs execute channel command words (CCWs) in memory, orchestrating complex multi-device I/O transfers with zero CPU intervention.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Asynchronous Data Transfer'?

options.text: Data transfer between two independent units that do NOT share a common global clock signal
Data transfer that only occurs at night
Data transfer that has no errors
Transferring data over the internet

explanation: Because transmitter and receiver use separate internal clocks, asynchronous communication requires handshaking or strobe control signals to coordinate data validity.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Strobe Control' in asynchronous data transfer?

options.text: A single control signal line (Strobe) asserted by either source or destination to indicate that data is available on the bus or has been accepted
A flashing light on the front panel
A timer that clicks every microsecond
A software command in C

explanation: In source-initiated strobe, the sender places data on the bus and pulses the strobe line. A fundamental flaw is the sender has no confirmation that the receiver actually received the data.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: How does the 'Two-Way Handshaking' protocol improve upon Strobe Control?

options.text: It uses two control lines: a Request signal from the sender and an Acknowledge signal from the receiver, guaranteeing mutual synchronization with zero data loss
It transfers data using two wires
It doubles the bus voltage
It requires user confirmation on screen

explanation: Handshaking provides full two-way interlocked feedback: Source asserts 'Data Ready', Destination reads data and asserts 'Data Accepted', Source drops 'Data Ready', and Destination drops 'Data Accepted'.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Synchronous Serial Transmission'?

options.text: Data bits are transmitted continuously at a fixed rate synchronized to a common shared clock signal, often framed with special sync characters (SYN)
Data sent with start and stop bits for each character
Data sent over parallel ribbon cables
Data stored on optical discs

explanation: Synchronous transmission sends continuous bit streams preceded by synchronization bit patterns, offering high line efficiency for bulk data transfers.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Asynchronous Serial Transmission' (e.g., UART / RS-232)?

options.text: Each character is framed individually with a Start Bit (logic 0), 7-8 Data Bits, an optional Parity Bit, and 1-2 Stop Bits (logic 1)
Data bits sent without any clock synchronization
Sending 1000 bytes in a single packet
Data sent using radio waves

explanation: In UART communication, lines idle at mark (logic 1); a falling edge start bit (0) alerts the receiver's local clock to sample subsequent bits, concluding with stop bits.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Baud Rate' in serial data communications?

options.text: The rate at which the signal line changes state (signal units / modulation symbols per second)
The number of files downloaded per second
The storage capacity of the hard drive
The voltage of the serial port

explanation: Baud measures signaling modulation events per second. If each signal event carries 1 bit, Baud rate equals Bits-Per-Second (bps).

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Parity Bit' in serial data transmission?

options.text: An additional check bit appended to a binary data word to make the total number of 1-bits either even (Even Parity) or odd (Odd Parity), enabling single-bit error detection
A bit that speeds up transmission
The most significant bit of an integer
A bit used to power the serial cable

explanation: Parity provides simple error detection: if an odd parity scheme receives a byte with an even number of 1-bits, a transmission error is flagged.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: In an asynchronous serial transmission at 9600 baud using 1 start bit, 8 data bits, no parity, and 1 stop bit (10 bits total per character), how many characters are transmitted per second?

options.text: 960 characters per second (9600 / 10 = 960)
9600 characters per second
1200 characters per second
800 characters per second

explanation: Each character consumes 10 frame bits. At 9600 bits per second: 9600 / 10 = 960 characters/second.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a 'UART' (Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter)?

options.text: An integrated circuit microchip that converts parallel data from the CPU bus into serial bit streams for transmission, and converts incoming serial streams back into parallel data
A universal power adapter
A software program that plays videos
A network router

explanation: UART handles parallel-to-serial serialization and serial-to-parallel deserialization, framing characters with start/stop bits and parity automatically.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a 'FIFO Buffer' inside a modern UART (e.g., 16550 UART)?

options.text: A first-in, first-out hardware queue (e.g., 16 or 64 bytes) that buffers incoming and outgoing bytes, preventing buffer overrun errors during high CPU load
A cache for CPU instructions
A memory stick for laptops
A circular magnetic disk

explanation: UART FIFOs buffer characters so the CPU does not need to service an interrupt for every single individual byte, reducing context switch load.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Direct Memory Access' (DMA) Bus Mastership?

options.text: The DMA controller takes over the system address, data, and control lines, acting as the bus master to drive memory cycles directly
The CPU controls the DMA controller
The hard drive operates without electricity
The monitor controls the bus

explanation: When the CPU grants bus access (Bus Grant BG asserted), the DMA controller acts as master, generating physical address and read/write pulses directly.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What handshaking signals are exchanged between the CPU and a DMA controller to transfer bus mastership?

options.text: Bus Request (BR) and Bus Grant (BG)
Start and Stop
Read and Write
Clock and Data

explanation: The DMAC asserts Bus Request (BR); upon reaching the end of the current machine cycle, the CPU asserts Bus Grant (BG) and floats its bus lines to high-impedance.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is an 'I/O Port'?

options.text: A specific register (Data, Control, or Status) inside an I/O device controller that can be read or written by the CPU via bus instructions
A physical hole on the back of the PC
A shipping dock for computers
A software program

explanation: At the architectural level, an I/O port is a hardware address assigned to a peripheral controller register.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: In an 8086 processor, how many 8-bit I/O ports can be directly addressed using the 16-bit port addressing capability?

options.text: 65,536 I/O ports (ports 0x0000 to 0xFFFF)
256 ports
1,024 ports

explanation: A 16-bit I/O port address space can address 2^16 = 65,536 distinct 8-bit I/O ports.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the primary difference between Memory-Mapped I/O and Isolated (Port-Mapped) I/O regarding CPU instruction sets?

options.text: Memory-Mapped I/O uses standard memory instructions (MOV, LOAD, STORE); Isolated I/O requires dedicated instructions (IN, OUT)
Memory-Mapped I/O can only write, never read
Isolated I/O cannot use registers
There is no difference in instructions

explanation: Memory-mapped I/O treats device registers as memory locations, using the full rich memory instruction set. Isolated I/O uses dedicated IN/OUT port instructions.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a major advantage of Memory-Mapped I/O?

options.text: Any instruction that can manipulate memory (arithmetic, logical, bit test) can operate directly on peripheral device registers without loading into AC first
It requires no address decoding
It makes RAM infinite
It eliminates all bus wires

explanation: Instructions like ADD M[Port], TEST M[Port] can directly process I/O registers without intermediate accumulator transfers.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a disadvantage of Memory-Mapped I/O?

options.text: Part of the physical memory address space is consumed by peripheral hardware registers, reducing total addressable RAM
It runs 10 times slower than port I/O
It causes memory bus short circuits
It can only be used on laptops

explanation: Allocating address ranges to I/O devices reduces the memory address space available for system RAM.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the difference between Simplex, Half-Duplex, and Full-Duplex communication channels?

options.text: Simplex: unidirectional only; Half-Duplex: bidirectional but only one direction at a time; Full-Duplex: simultaneous bidirectional transmission
Simplex has one wire; Full-Duplex has 100 wires
Half-Duplex is half speed; Full-Duplex is full speed
There is no distinction

explanation: Simplex is one-way (radio broadcast); Half-Duplex is two-way alternate (walkie-talkie); Full-Duplex is simultaneous two-way (telephone).

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is an 'Edge-Triggered Interrupt' vs a 'Level-Triggered Interrupt'?

options.text: Edge-triggered detects a voltage transition (low-to-high or high-to-low); Level-triggered detects a sustained logic voltage level (logic 0 or logic 1)
Edge-triggered only works on monitors
Level-triggered is an analog signal
There is no functional difference

explanation: Edge-triggered latches on the pulse edge (avoids repeated interrupts if line stays high); level-triggered requires the device to clear the line before ISR completes.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a 'Spurious Interrupt'?

options.text: A glitch or transient electrical noise on an interrupt line that triggers an interrupt cycle even though no hardware device requested service
An interrupt caused by a hacker
A planned diagnostic interrupt
An interrupt that formats the hard drive

explanation: If electrical noise pulses an interrupt line, the CPU enters the interrupt cycle but finds no device asserting a request (e.g., IRQ7 on legacy x86 PIC).

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the 'PIC' (Programmable Interrupt Controller, e.g., Intel 8259A)?

options.text: A dedicated chip that manages, prioritizes, and cascades multiple hardware interrupt lines, presenting a single INT request to the CPU
A microcontroller for cameras
A chip that controls the power supply
A network router

explanation: The 8259A PIC aggregates 8 interrupt lines (expandable to 64 via cascading master-slave configuration), resolving priorities and asserting the CPU INT pin.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the function of the APIC (Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller) in modern multi-core x86 systems?

options.text: Distributes hardware interrupts dynamically across multiple CPU cores and supports Inter-Processor Interrupts (IPIs) for inter-core communication
Controls the monitor backlight
Formats SSD drives
Runs the BIOS setup utility

explanation: APIC (Local APIC per core + I/O APIC) routes peripheral interrupts to specific cores and enables cores to interrupt each other via IPIs.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Inter-Processor Interrupt' (IPI)?

options.text: A special hardware interrupt sent by one CPU core to another CPU core to coordinate scheduling, cache flushing, or task migration
An interrupt from a USB mouse
A power saving sleep signal
A software bug

explanation: IPIs are essential in multi-core operating systems for TLB shootdowns, cross-core scheduling, and thread preemption.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: In an RS-232 serial interface, what do the signals RTS and CTS stand for?

options.text: Request To Send (RTS) and Clear To Send (CTS) - hardware flow control signals
Ready To Start and Close The Socket
Run Time System and Compile Time System
Reset The System and Clear The Screen

explanation: RTS and CTS provide out-of-band hardware flow control: sender asserts RTS, receiver responds with CTS when ready to buffer bytes.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'Software Flow Control' in serial communications using XON and XOFF characters?

options.text: The receiver sends ASCII XOFF (Ctrl-S, 0x13) to pause the sender when its buffer is full, and sends XON (Ctrl-Q, 0x11) to resume transmission
Using passwords to control file transfers
Controlling CPU clock speed via software
A firewall utility

explanation: In-band software flow control embeds special control characters (XON/XOFF) within the data stream, eliminating dedicated control wires.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'USB' (Universal Serial Bus) architecture?

options.text: A tiered-star topology serial bus providing plug-and-play peripheral connectivity, packetized communication, and power delivery over 4+ wires
A parallel bus inside hard drives
A wireless protocol for keyboards
A storage disk format

explanation: USB connects peripherals to a host controller via hubs, offering hot-swapping, tiered-star topology, and standardized device classes.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the maximum number of devices that can be attached to a single USB host controller tier?

options.text: Up to 127 devices (using 7-bit device address field)
Up to 16 devices
Up to 256 devices
Up to 64 devices

explanation: The USB specification reserves a 7-bit device address, allowing up to 127 unique peripheral endpoints per host controller.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is 'PCIe' (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express)?

options.text: A high-speed serial point-to-point interconnect standard using dedicated differential signaling Lanes (x1, x4, x8, x16) for graphics and NVMe devices
An old parallel printer bus
A software protocol for web pages
A power cable specification

explanation: PCIe replaced legacy shared parallel PCI with scalable point-to-point serial lanes, delivering tens of gigabytes per second of bandwidth.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is an 'I/O Bus Cycle'?

options.text: The time interval required to transfer one word between the CPU/DMA and an I/O device controller register
The time to boot the computer
The refresh rate of the monitor
The clock cycle of the CPU ALU

explanation: An I/O cycle executes on the system bus when addressing I/O ports or device controller registers, typically taking longer than memory bus cycles.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the fundamental trade-off between 'Burst Mode' and 'Cycle Stealing' in DMA data transfer?

options.text: Burst mode provides maximum data transfer speed by holding the bus continuously, but blocks the CPU; Cycle Stealing interleaves words, allowing the CPU to execute concurrently
Burst mode is slower than polling
Cycle stealing destroys memory data
There is no trade-off

explanation: Burst mode minimizes total block transfer time at the expense of locking out the CPU. Cycle stealing leaves the CPU responsive with minimal interference.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: In Daisy Chaining priority interrupt resolution, which device possesses the highest priority?

options.text: The device physically connected closest to the CPU (first in the serial INTA chain)
The device with the highest model number
The device that consumes the most power
The device farthest from the CPU

explanation: In daisy-chaining, priority is hardwired by physical proximity to the interrupt acknowledge pin: the first device intercepts the grant signal first.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: In Parallel Priority Interrupt systems, what digital logic circuit identifies the highest priority requesting device?

options.text: Priority Encoder circuit
Half Adder circuit
Multiplexer
Shift register

explanation: A Priority Encoder accepts multiple active request inputs and outputs the binary address of the highest-order active bit.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a 'Non-Maskable Interrupt' (NMI)?

options.text: A critical hardware interrupt that CANNOT be disabled or ignored by CPU software instructions, reserved for catastrophic hardware emergencies (e.g., bus parity error, imminent power failure)
An interrupt caused by a user mouse click
An interrupt from a USB printer
An interrupt with zero priority

explanation: NMI lines bypass software interrupt mask flags, guaranteeing immediate CPU response during catastrophic hardware faults.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: Why is an oversampling clock (e.g., 16x baud rate clock) used in UART serial receivers?

options.text: To detect the falling edge of the Start Bit reliably and sample subsequent data bits precisely at their middle to maximize noise margin
To speed up the internet
To save electrical energy
To double the baud rate

explanation: A 16x clock samples the start bit at ticks 7-8 to verify it is not noise, then samples each data bit at its exact midpoint (tick 16) for reliable decoding.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is a 'Direct Memory Access' (DMA) channel multiplexer?

options.text: A hardware circuit allowing a single DMA controller chip to service multiple independent peripheral devices (e.g., Channels 0 through 3)
A tool for merging two files on disk
A video splitter
A cable with multiple heads

explanation: DMAC chips (like the classic Intel 8237) feature multiple independent DMA channels, each maintaining its own address and word count registers.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the communication protocol between the host CPU and an Input-Output Processor (IOP)?

options.text: The CPU places an I/O program in memory and issues a Start I/O signal; the IOP executes the channel program autonomously and interrupts the CPU upon completion
The CPU executes every instruction for the IOP
The IOP cannot read memory
Communication occurs via Bluetooth

explanation: The host CPU delegates entire complex transfer jobs by issuing START I/O; the IOP independently executes Channel Command Words (CCWs) and posts an interrupt upon completion.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: What is the primary role of the 'Interrupt Vector Table' (IVT)?

options.text: An array stored in low memory containing the memory entry point addresses of Interrupt Service Routines indexed by interrupt type
A table of user passwords
A list of CPU instructions
A directory of hard drive files

explanation: The IVT stores starting addresses of ISRs: the interrupt number multiplies by the vector size to look up the target address.

unit_title: Input/Output Organization, Interfaces & Data Transfer Modes
prompt: Why is I/O Organization crucial in modern system architecture?

options.text: Without efficient I/O subsystems and DMA, high-speed multi-gigahertz processors would remain idle waiting for human inputs and storage disks
Because I/O devices use more electricity than CPUs
Because computers only do input and output
Because monitors cannot work without I/O

explanation: Balanced I/O architecture ensures that immense CPU computing power translates to high overall application throughput.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Parallel Processing' in computer architecture?

options.text: Performing multiple computational tasks concurrently, using multiple functional units or processors, to increase overall system throughput
Running a single program very slowly
Using two monitors on one desk
Writing code in two languages simultaneously

explanation: Parallel processing exploits spatial parallelism (multiple hardware units) or temporal parallelism (overlapping pipeline stages) to accelerate computation.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Flynn's Taxonomy' of computer architectures?

options.text: A classification of computer systems into four categories based on the number of concurrent Instruction Streams and Data Streams
A classification of computer monitors
A system for rating CPU clock speeds
A hierarchy of memory chips

explanation: Michael J. Flynn proposed classifying architectures by Instruction and Data streams: SISD, SIMD, MISD, and MIMD.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What does 'SISD' stand for in Flynn's taxonomy?

options.text: Single Instruction Single Data stream (classic Von Neumann uniprocessor)
Serial Instruction Serial Data
Synchronous Interface Serial Driver
Standard Instruction Set Device

explanation: SISD is the conventional single-core processor executing one instruction at a time on a single data operand stream.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What does 'SIMD' stand for, and what type of computing architectures exemplify it?

options.text: Single Instruction Multiple Data stream: a single instruction controls multiple processing elements operating on different data vectors simultaneously (e.g., Vector processors, GPUs)
Serial Interface Multi-Device
Synchronous Instruction Memory Driver
Single Integrated Motherboard Design

explanation: SIMD processors broadcast a single instruction across an array of ALUs, executing the same operation (e.g., vector addition) on parallel data streams simultaneously.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What does 'MISD' stand for in Flynn's taxonomy?

options.text: Multiple Instruction Single Data stream (rarely implemented, used in specialized fault-tolerant aerospace voting systems)
Microprocessor Instruction Storage Device
Mainframe Integrated Serial Drive
Multi-core Interface Synchronous Driver

explanation: MISD feeds a single data stream through multiple independent processors executing different instruction streams (e.g., triple-modular redundancy in flight computers).

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What does 'MIMD' stand for, and what type of computers represent it?

options.text: Multiple Instruction Multiple Data stream: multiple independent processors executing different instructions on different datasets concurrently (e.g., Multi-core CPUs, Clusters)
Master Instruction Multi-Device
Mega Instruction Memory Design
Mainframe Interconnect Modular Design

explanation: MIMD encompasses all modern multi-core microprocessors, distributed clusters, and supercomputers where cores operate autonomously.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Pipelining' in CPU execution, and what classic manufacturing analogy explains it?

options.text: Overlapping the execution of successive instructions across segmented hardware stages, analogous to an industrial automobile assembly line
Pumping cooling liquid through copper pipes
Sending instructions through pneumatic tubes
A method for sorting numbers on paper

explanation: Like an assembly line where each station performs one task on a car as it moves along, pipelining executes different sub-operations on successive instructions concurrently.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: If a non-pipelined processor executes an instruction in time t_n = 50 ns, what is the total time to execute 1,000 instructions?

options.text: 50,000 ns (50 microseconds)
500 ns

explanation: Total non-pipelined time T_1 = n * t_n = 1000 * 50 ns = 50,000 ns.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: In a k-segment pipeline with clock cycle time t_k, what is the total time T_k required to execute n independent instructions?

options.text: T_k = (k + n - 1) * t_k
T_k = k * n * t_k
T_k = (n / k) * t_k
T_k = (k - n) * t_k

explanation: The first instruction takes k clock cycles to fill the pipeline; each subsequent (n - 1) instruction completes in 1 cycle: Total Cycles = k + n - 1.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is the formula for the 'Speedup Ratio' (S_k) of a k-segment pipeline over a non-pipelined processor?

options.text: S_k = k * n
S_k = t_n / t_k

explanation: Speedup S_k is the ratio of non-pipelined time to pipelined time: S_k = (n * t_n) / [(k + n - 1) * t_k].

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: As the number of instructions n approaches infinity (n -> infinity), what is the maximum theoretical speedup of a k-stage pipeline (assuming t_n = k * t_k)?

options.text: k (equal to the number of pipeline stages)
Infinity

explanation: As n -> inf, (n / (k + n - 1)) -> 1. If t_n = k * t_k, maximum theoretical speedup S_max = k.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Pipeline Efficiency' (E)?

options.text: The ratio of actual speedup achieved to the maximum theoretical speedup: E = S_k / k
The clock speed of the pipeline in GHz
The temperature of the pipeline
The power consumed per instruction

explanation: Efficiency E = S_k / k measures how fully utilized all pipeline stages are across execution (E approaches 1 as n grows large).

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is an 'Arithmetic Pipeline'?

options.text: A segmented pipeline designed to execute multi-step arithmetic calculations (e.g., floating-point addition or multiplication) across cascaded stages
A pipeline that executes jumps and branches
A pipe that carries numbers
An algorithm written in assembly

explanation: Arithmetic pipelines partition complex numeric operations (e.g., floating-point add: compare exponents, align mantissa, add mantissas, normalize) into high-speed stages.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What are the four standard sequential stages of a Floating-Point Addition pipeline?

options.text: 1. Compare exponents -> 2. Align mantissas -> 3. Add/subtract mantissas -> 4. Normalize the result
1. Multiply -> 2. Divide -> 3. Add -> 4. Subtract
1. Round -> 2. Truncate -> 3. Shift -> 4. Clear
1. Load -> 2. Decode -> 3. Execute -> 4. Store

explanation: Floating-point addition requires aligning radix points before addition and renormalizing the significand and adjusting exponents afterward.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What are the four typical stages of a classic RISC Instruction Pipeline?

options.text: Fetch Instruction (FI) -> Decode Instruction (DA) -> Fetch Operand (FO) -> Execute Instruction (EX)
Power on -> Read disk -> Print -> Power off
Compile -> Link -> Assemble -> Run
Read -> Write -> Verify -> Clear

explanation: Classic 4-stage pipelines partition execution into: Fetch instruction, Decode/register read, Operand fetch/ALU, and Writeback/store.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Pipeline Hazard'?

options.text: Any condition that prevents the next instruction in the instruction stream from executing in its designated clock cycle, causing pipeline stalls (bubbles)
A physical fire on the motherboard
A short circuit in the power supply
A virus in the instruction cache

explanation: Pipeline hazards disrupt smooth overlapped execution, forcing the insertion of idle clock cycles (bubbles / stalls) and degrading throughput.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What are the THREE major categories of Pipeline Hazards?

options.text: Structural Hazards, Data Hazards, and Control (Branch) Hazards
Voltage Hazards, Heat Hazards, and Noise Hazards
Input Hazards, Output Hazards, and Storage Hazards
Compile Hazards, Link Hazards, and Load Hazards

explanation: 1. Structural (resource conflict), 2. Data (operand dependency), and 3. Control (branching/program flow change).

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What causes a 'Structural Hazard' (Resource Hazard)?

options.text: Two or more pipeline stages attempt to access the exact same physical hardware resource simultaneously (e.g., single memory port for instruction fetch and data read)
A compiler error
An invalid opcode
A low battery voltage

explanation: Structural hazards occur when hardware lacks sufficient duplication (e.g., Von Neumann unified memory accessed by FI and FO simultaneously, resolvable by Harvard dual caches).

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What causes a 'Data Hazard' (Data Dependency)?

options.text: An instruction depends on the result of a previous instruction that is still in flight in the pipeline and has not yet written its result to the register file
Corrupted data on the hard drive
An integer overflow
A parity error on the bus

explanation: Data hazards arise when instructions exhibit read/write dependencies on registers being modified by preceding instructions.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Read-After-Write' (RAW) Data Hazard (True Data Dependency)?

options.text: Instruction j attempts to read a register before instruction i writes to it (j tries to read old/stale data)
Instruction j writes before i reads
Instruction j writes before i writes
Instruction j reads before i reads

explanation: RAW is a true dependency: i: R1 <- R2 + R3; j: R4 <- R1 + R5. Instruction j needs R1 produced by i. If j reads R1 before i completes writeback, j gets corrupt data.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Operand Forwarding' (Bypassing) to resolve RAW data hazards?

options.text: Routing the calculated ALU result directly from the output of the execution stage back to the input of the next stage without waiting for register writeback
Writing operands to disk
Skipping the dependent instruction
Pausing the CPU for 10 cycles

explanation: Operand forwarding intercepts newly computed results at the ALU output register and forwards them directly to the next stage's ALU input multiplexer, eliminating pipeline stalls.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Control Hazard' (Branch Hazard)?

options.text: A hazard caused by conditional or unconditional branch instructions that alter the Program Counter, rendering already fetched instructions in the pipeline invalid
A hardware switch failure
A power outage
A failure in the clock circuit

explanation: When a branch is taken, instructions fetched sequentially behind the branch must be discarded (flushed), resulting in branch penalty delay cycles.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Pipeline Stall' (Bubble)?

options.text: An idle clock cycle inserted into a pipeline stage where no productive instruction advances, allowing a dependency or conflict to resolve
A bubble in the liquid cooling system
A circular graphic on screen
A paused background thread

explanation: A stall (bubble) holds upstream pipeline stages motionless while downstream stages advance, draining dependencies.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Delayed Branching' used in RISC architectures to mitigate control hazards?

options.text: The compiler places a useful, independent instruction in the 'Branch Delay Slot' immediately following the branch, which is ALWAYS executed regardless of branch outcome
Delaying the computer reboot
Waiting 5 seconds before jumping
Executing branches only at the end of the program

explanation: The branch delay slot is always executed while the branch target address is being computed, converting would-be wasted stall cycles into useful work.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Branch Prediction' in modern high-performance microprocessors?

options.text: Hardware logic that guesses whether a conditional branch will be Taken or Not-Taken before the condition is evaluated, allowing speculative instruction fetching
Asking the user which way to branch
A random coin toss in silicon
A compiler diagnostic report

explanation: Branch predictors (static or dynamic via Branch Target Buffers and 2-bit saturating counters) predict branch outcomes with >95% accuracy to prevent pipeline flushes.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Speculative Execution'?

options.text: The CPU fetches, decodes, and executes instructions along a predicted branch path before knowing for certain whether the branch will actually be taken
Buying computer hardware on credit
Running code without compiling it
Executing code with unknown results

explanation: Speculative execution keeps execution units busy: if the branch prediction is correct, results commit immediately; if mispredicted, speculative results are squashed.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What does Amdahl's Law state regarding the speedup achievable by parallel processing?

options.text: The overall speedup of a system is strictly limited by the fraction of the program that must be executed serially (the sequential bottleneck)
Adding more CPUs always doubles system speed
Hardware never fails
Parallel computing uses zero power

explanation: Amdahl's Law states: Speedup = 1 / ((1 - P) + P / N), where P is the parallelizable fraction and N is processor count. If 10% is strictly serial, maximum possible speedup cannot exceed 10x, even with infinite CPUs.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: According to Amdahl's Law, if 80% of a program can be parallelized (P = 0.8) and 20% is strictly sequential, what is the MAXIMUM theoretical speedup with an INFINITE number of processors?

options.text: 5x (Speedup = 1 / 0.20 = 5)
Infinite speedup

explanation: As N -> inf, P/N -> 0. Max Speedup = 1 / (1 - P) = 1 / (1 - 0.80) = 1 / 0.20 = 5x. The 20% serial fraction caps speedup at 5x.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Gustafson's Law' (Scaled Speedup) in parallel computing?

options.text: As more processors become available, the problem size scales up proportionally, allowing parallel work to dominate and overcoming Amdahl's pessimistic limit
Computers get smaller every two years
Network speed increases linearly
Storage capacity doubles annually

explanation: Gustafson observed that scientists don't run small problems on supercomputers; they solve massively larger problems where the serial fraction shrinks towards zero: Scaled Speedup = s + p*N.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Tightly Coupled Multiprocessor' (Shared-Memory Multiprocessor / UMA)?

options.text: Multiple processors sharing a common physical memory and single operating system over a high-speed bus, with uniform memory access latency (UMA)
Computers tied together with metal wire
Independent computers communicating via internet
A single core with two ALUs

explanation: In tightly coupled systems, all CPUs share a unified physical address space and main memory with identical access times (Uniform Memory Access).

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'NUMA' (Non-Uniform Memory Access) architecture?

options.text: A shared-memory multiprocessor system where access time to memory varies depending on whether the memory is local to the accessing processor or remote on another socket
A system with no memory
A system where all memory access takes equal time
A hard drive RAID array

explanation: In NUMA servers, each CPU socket has dedicated local memory; accessing local memory is fast, while accessing remote memory across QPI/interconnect incurs higher latency.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Loosely Coupled Multiprocessor' (Distributed-Memory System / Cluster)?

options.text: Multiple autonomous computer nodes, each with its own private local memory and OS, communicating exclusively via message passing across a network
A computer with loose cables
A laptop with multiple flash drives
A CPU with disconnected cores

explanation: Loosely coupled systems (clusters, MPPs) share no common physical memory, coordinating work through message passing libraries like MPI.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Vector Processing' in supercomputing?

options.text: Hardware capable of performing arithmetic operations on entire 1D arrays (vectors) of numbers in a single machine instruction (e.g., C = A + B for 64-element vectors)
Processing graphics vectors on screen
A method for drawing lines in CAD
A network routing algorithm

explanation: Vector processors feature vector registers and pipelined vector ALUs that process entire arrays in a single pipelined instruction stream without loop branch overhead.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Strip-Mining' in vector compiler optimization?

options.text: Dividing a large vector loop of arbitrary length N into chunks that match the hardware vector register length (e.g., chunks of 64)
Mining cryptocurrency on GPUs
Stripping comments from assembly code
Erasing disk tracks

explanation: Strip-mining breaks loops with length N > Vector_Register_Length into manageable batches fitting physical hardware vector registers.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'GPU' (Graphics Processing Unit) compared to a CPU?

options.text: A massively parallel processor consisting of thousands of small, efficient cores optimized for high-throughput arithmetic on massive data parallel arrays (SIMD/SIMT)
A chip that only displays desktop icons
A faster version of a single-core CPU
A power supply regulator

explanation: While CPUs optimize low-latency sequential thread execution with massive caches, GPUs dedicate silicon to thousands of ALUs delivering teraflops of parallel throughput.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is the 'Crossbar Switch' interconnection network in multiprocessors?

options.text: A dynamic network connecting n processors to m memory modules using n x m cross-point switches, allowing non-blocking concurrent access as long as no two CPUs access the same module
A network crossing international borders
A serial RS-232 cable
A network with only one wire

explanation: Crossbar switches provide complete point-to-point non-blocking connectivity, but hardware complexity grows as O(n * m), becoming expensive for large node counts.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is an 'Omega Network' (Multistage Interconnection Network - MIN)?

options.text: A network of 2x2 switching elements arranged in log_2(N) stages using perfect-shuffle permutations to route N inputs to N outputs
A Greek computer network
The final computer on a LAN
A network with infinite bandwidth

explanation: Omega networks achieve scalable cost O(N * log N) using cascaded shuffle-exchange stages between processors and memory banks.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Hypercube' (Binary n-cube) interconnection topology for 2^n nodes?

options.text: A network where each node is connected to n neighbors, corresponding to the corners of an n-dimensional cube, with maximum communication distance of n hops
A 3D cardboard box
A circular token ring
A star network around a central server

explanation: In a hypercube of dimension n, 2^n nodes have diameter n (e.g., 8-cube has 256 nodes, any two nodes within 8 hops), providing high bisection bandwidth.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Cache Invalidation Traffic' in bus-snooping multiprocessor systems?

options.text: Broadcast signals sent across the shared bus whenever a processor modifies a shared variable, alerting other cores to invalidate their local copies
Downloading files from the web
Clearing web browser cookies
Power consumption spikes

explanation: In write-invalidate protocols, every write to a shared line requires broadcasting an invalidation address, which can saturate the shared bus on high core counts.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Instruction-Level Parallelism' (ILP)?

options.text: The potential overlap and simultaneous execution of multiple independent instructions within a single program instruction stream
Connecting multiple instruction registers in parallel
Running multiple operating systems at once
Printing assembly code side-by-side

explanation: Pipelining, superscalar execution, out-of-order execution, and VLIW architectures exploit ILP to execute multiple instructions per cycle.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Very Long Instruction Word' (VLIW) processor architecture?

options.text: The compiler statically groups multiple independent operations into a single massive instruction word executed concurrently by execution units without hardware dependency checking
Instructions with 1000 characters of text
A processor that executes one instruction per hour
A computer with a giant screen

explanation: VLIW shifts dependency analysis entirely from hardware to the optimizing compiler, packing multiple operations into a wide instruction word.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Out-of-Order Execution' (OoO) in modern superscalar processors?

options.text: Instructions execute as soon as their operand data is available in reservation stations, rather than strictly in original program sequence
Executing instructions backwards
Random instruction execution
Executing code after shutdown

explanation: OoO dynamically reorders instructions using scoreboarding or Tomasulo's algorithm to prevent pipeline stalls while instructions wait for slow cache misses.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Branch Target Buffer' (BTB)?

options.text: A high-speed cache that stores the target addresses of previously executed branch instructions, enabling zero-cycle target address fetch before instruction decode
A buffer that stores tree branches
A temporary stack pointer
A USB buffer

explanation: The BTB caches branch instructions alongside their predicted targets, allowing the fetch unit to immediately redirect the instruction stream without decode delay.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Write-After-Write' (WAW) Output Dependency?

options.text: Instruction j writes to register R after instruction i writes to register R; out-of-order execution must ensure the final value in R matches the latter write
Two instructions reading the same register
A write to two different files
An instruction that never finishes

explanation: WAW is an output dependency where instruction order must be preserved to guarantee the register holds the correct terminal value.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is a 'Write-After-Read' (WAR) Anti-Dependency?

options.text: Instruction j writes to register R before instruction i has read its previous value from R
Instruction j reads before i writes
An infinite loop
A memory bus error

explanation: WAR occurs when an instruction overwrites an operand needed by an earlier in-flight instruction.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: How does 'Register Renaming' eliminate false WAR and WAW dependencies in superscalar processors?

options.text: It maps architectural register names dynamically to a much larger pool of physical rename registers, breaking name conflicts
It renames variables in source code
It changes file extensions
It assigns random numbers to registers

explanation: Register renaming breaks false name dependencies (WAR, WAW) by assigning fresh physical registers to every new write, allowing instructions to execute in parallel.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'SIMT' (Single Instruction, Multiple Threads) used in GPU compute architectures?

options.text: An execution model where groups of threads (Warps / Wavefronts) execute the same instruction in lockstep across SIMD execution lanes
Running multiple operating systems on one core
Single thread running multiple programs
Serial execution on single ALU

explanation: SIMT combines thread-level programming with SIMD hardware execution: instructions are broadcast across a warp (32 threads in NVIDIA CUDA).

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: What is 'Massively Parallel Processing' (MPP)?

options.text: A supercomputing architecture consisting of hundreds or thousands of independent processing nodes with separate memory, interconnected by high-speed proprietary fabrics
A PC with two graphics cards
A dual-core laptop
A web browser with 50 tabs

explanation: MPP systems are large-scale distributed-memory supercomputers executing parallel programs via message passing without shared memory contention.

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: In a 4-stage arithmetic pipeline with clock cycle time t_k = 10 ns, what is the time taken to process 100 inputs?

options.text: 400 ns

explanation: Time T_k = (k + n - 1) * t_k = (4 + 100 - 1) * 10 ns = 103 * 10 ns = 1,030 ns. (Compare with non-pipelined time 40 ns * 100 = 4,000 ns).

unit_title: Parallel Processing, Pipelining & Multiprocessor Systems
prompt: Why did the computer industry shift from increasing single-core clock frequency to multi-core parallel architecture?

options.text: Due to the 'Power Wall' (thermal dissipation limits) and the breakdown of Dennard Scaling, making further single-core clock scaling power-inefficient
Because multi-core CPUs are cheaper to manufacture
Because single-core CPUs ran out of numbers
Because software became too simple

explanation: Power dissipation increases cubically with clock frequency (P ≈ C * V^2 * f). Hitting thermal limits forced the paradigm shift to multi-core parallelism.
